```{r}
library(tidyverse)
library(patchwork)
library(p8105.datasets)
```

## Problem 1
### Data cleaning and description

```{r}
data("ny_noaa")

noaa_df =
  ny_noaa |>
  mutate(
    year = lubridate::year(date),
    month = lubridate::month(date),
    day = lubridate::day(date),
    tmax = as.numeric(tmax) / 10,
    tmin = as.numeric(tmin) / 10,
    prcp = prcp / 10
  )
```

The original dataset contains `r nrow(ny_noaa)` observations and
`r ncol(ny_noaa)` variables from `r n_distinct(ny_noaa$id)` weather
stations in New York. Each observation represents weather measurements
for one station on one date. The data include precipitation, snowfall,
snow depth, and maximum and minimum temperatures.

```{r}
noaa_df |>
  summarise(
    across(
      c(prcp, snow, snwd, tmax, tmin),
      ~ mean(is.na(.x)) * 100
    )
  ) |>
  pivot_longer(
    everything(),
    names_to = "variable",
    values_to = "missing_percent"
  ) |>
  knitr::kable(
    digits = 1,
    col.names = c("Variable", "Missing (%)")
  )
```
Both maximum and minimum temperatures are missing for 43.7% of observations.
Snow depth is missing for 22.8%, snowfall for 14.7%, and precipitation
for 5.6%. Therefore, summaries and plots based on observed values may
not fully represent all stations and dates.

### Most common snowfall values

```{r}
noaa_df |>
  filter(!is.na(snow)) |>
  count(snow, sort = TRUE) |>
  slice_head(n = 10) |>
  knitr::kable(
    col.names = c("Snowfall (mm)", "Number of observations")
  )
```
The most common snowfall value is 0 mm, with 2,008,508 observations,
because most station-days have no snowfall. Other common values include
25, 13, and 51 mm. These values are approximately 1, 0.5, and 2 inches,
suggesting that measurements originally recorded in inches were
converted to millimeters and rounded.

### Average maximum temperature in January and July

```{r, fig.width=10, fig.height=5}
noaa_monthly =
  noaa_df |>
  filter(month %in% c(1, 7)) |>
  group_by(id, year, month) |>
  summarise(
    mean_tmax = mean(tmax, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  filter(!is.na(mean_tmax)) |>
  mutate(
    month = factor(
      month,
      levels = c(1, 7),
      labels = c("January", "July")
    )
  )

noaa_monthly |>
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = mean_tmax, group = id)) +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.2, color = "steelblue") +
  facet_wrap(~ month) +
  labs(
    title = "Average Maximum Temperature by Station and Year",
    x = "Year",
    y = "Average maximum temperature (°C)"
  )
```
Average maximum temperatures are much higher in July than in January.
January also shows larger year-to-year fluctuations. Many stations
follow similar patterns across years, suggesting shared regional
weather patterns. There are some possible outliers, including a July
average near 14°C around 1988, well below the other stations. Unusual
values may reflect local conditions, incomplete observations, or
recording errors and would require further investigation.

### Temperature relationship and snowfall distributions

```{r, fig.width=10, fig.height=10}
temp_plot =
  noaa_df |>
  filter(!is.na(tmax), !is.na(tmin)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = tmin, y = tmax)) +
  geom_bin_2d(bins = 60) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(trans = "log10") +
  labs(
    title = "Maximum versus Minimum Temperature",
    x = "Minimum temperature (°C)",
    y = "Maximum temperature (°C)",
    fill = "Count"
  )

snow_plot =
  noaa_df |>
  filter(snow > 0, snow < 100) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = factor(year), y = snow)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.size = 0.5) +
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of Snowfall by Year",
    x = "Year",
    y = "Snowfall (mm)"
  ) +
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 90, hjust = 1)
  )

temp_plot / snow_plot
```
Maximum and minimum temperatures show a strong positive relationship:
days with higher minimum temperatures generally also have higher
maximum temperatures. A few observations have extreme temperatures,
and some appear to have maximum temperatures below minimum
temperatures, suggesting possible recording errors.

For snowfall values greater than 0 and less than 100 mm, the
distributions are similar across years. The median is approximately
25 mm in each year, and the middle 50% of observations generally fall
between about 13 and 51 mm. Some years, such as 2006, have a smaller
interquartile range. There is no clear long-term trend in these
conditional snowfall distributions.

## Problem 2
### Import and clean the data

```{r}
covar_df =
  read_csv("data/nhanes_covar.csv", skip = 4) |>
  janitor::clean_names() |>
  filter(age >= 21) |>
  drop_na(sex, age, bmi, education) |>
  mutate(
    sex = factor(
      sex,
      levels = c(1, 2),
      labels = c("Male", "Female")
    ),
    education = factor(
      education,
      levels = c(1, 2, 3),
      labels = c(
        "Less than high school",
        "High school equivalent",
        "More than high school"
      )
    )
  )

accel_df =
  read_csv("data/nhanes_accel.csv") |>
  janitor::clean_names()

nhanes_df =
  covar_df |>
  left_join(accel_df, by = "seqn") |>
  pivot_longer(
    starts_with("min"),
    names_to = "minute",
    names_prefix = "min",
    values_to = "mims"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    minute = as.integer(minute),
    hour = (minute - 1) / 60
  )
```

Participants younger than 21 years and those with missing demographic
data were excluded. Sex and education were converted to factors with
descriptive labels. The demographic and activity datasets were merged
using participant ID. Minute-level activity measurements were then
converted from wide to long format, retaining all original demographic
variables.

The cleaned dataset includes `r nrow(covar_df)` participants.
Each row of the merged, tidy dataset represents one minute for one
participant. Minute 1 corresponds to midnight.

### Number of participants by sex and education

```{r}
covar_df |>
  count(education, sex) |>
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = sex,
    values_from = n,
    values_fill = 0
  ) |>
  knitr::kable(
    col.names = c("Education", "Male", "Female")
  )
```

The more than high school group has the most participants, with 56 men
and 59 women. The less than high school group has similar numbers of
men and women (27 and 28), while the high school equivalent group has
more men than women (35 versus 23).

### Age distributions by sex and education

```{r, fig.width=10, fig.height=5}
covar_df |>
  ggplot(aes(x = sex, y = age, fill = sex)) +
  geom_boxplot(width = 0.5) +
  facet_wrap(
    ~ education,
    labeller = label_wrap_gen(width = 20)
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Age Distributions by Sex and Education",
    x = "Sex",
    y = "Age (years)"
  ) +
  guides(fill = "none")
```
Participants with more than high school education are generally younger,
with median ages of approximately 44 for men and 41 for women. In the
less than high school group, men and women have similar age distributions,
with medians around 60. In the high school equivalent group, women have
a higher median age than men, approximately 62 versus 53. However, age
distributions overlap substantially across groups.

### Total daily activity and age

```{r, fig.width=10, fig.height=5}
activity_total =
  nhanes_df |>
  group_by(seqn, sex, age, bmi, education) |>
  summarise(
    total_activity = sum(mims),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

activity_total |>
  ggplot(aes(x = age, y = total_activity, color = sex)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_smooth(method = "loess", se = FALSE) +
  facet_wrap(
    ~ education,
    labeller = label_wrap_gen(width = 20)
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Total Daily Activity and Age",
    x = "Age (years)",
    y = "Total daily activity (sum of MIMS)",
    color = "Sex"
  )
```
Total daily activity generally decreases with age across all three
education groups, although the relationships are not strictly linear.
In the less than high school group, men tend to have higher fitted
activity levels during middle age. In the high school equivalent group,
women have higher fitted activity levels around ages 30–50. In the more
than high school group, women generally have higher fitted activity
levels across most ages. There is considerable individual variation,
and these descriptive patterns do not establish causal relationships.
### Activity patterns over 24 hours

```{r, fig.width=10, fig.height=5}
activity_time =
  nhanes_df |>
  group_by(education, sex, minute, hour) |>
  summarise(
    mean_mims = mean(mims),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

activity_time |>
  ggplot(aes(x = hour, y = mean_mims, color = sex)) +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.3) +
  geom_smooth(
    method = "loess",
    span = 0.15,
    se = FALSE
  ) +
  facet_wrap(
    ~ education,
    labeller = label_wrap_gen(width = 20)
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    breaks = c(0, 6, 12, 18, 24),
    limits = c(0, 24)
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Activity Patterns over 24 Hours",
    x = "Hours since midnight",
    y = "Mean activity (MIMS)",
    color = "Sex"
  )
```
All three education groups show low activity overnight, a sharp increase
in the morning, higher activity during the day, and a decline in the
evening. In the less than high school group, activity peaks around late
morning, and men and women have similar daytime patterns. In the high
school equivalent group, women generally have higher activity during
the late morning and early afternoon. The more than high school group
shows a clearer sex difference, with women having higher average
activity throughout most daytime hours. These comparisons are
descriptive and may partly reflect differences in age across groups.

## Problem 3
### Import and clean the data

```{r}
jan_2020 =
  read_csv("data/Jan 2020 Citi.csv") |>
  mutate(year = 2020, month = "January")

july_2020 =
  read_csv("data/July 2020 Citi.csv") |>
  mutate(year = 2020, month = "July")

jan_2024 =
  read_csv("data/Jan 2024 Citi.csv") |>
  mutate(year = 2024, month = "January")

july_2024 =
  read_csv("data/July 2024 Citi.csv") |>
  mutate(year = 2024, month = "July")

citi_df =
  bind_rows(jan_2020, july_2020, jan_2024, july_2024) |>
  janitor::clean_names() |>
  mutate(
    year = factor(year),
    month = factor(
      month,
      levels = c("January", "July")
    ),
    weekdays = factor(
      weekdays,
      levels = c(
        "Monday", "Tuesday", "Wednesday", "Thursday",
        "Friday", "Saturday", "Sunday"
      )
    ),
    member_casual = factor(
      member_casual,
      levels = c("casual", "member"),
      labels = c("Casual", "Member")
    ),
    rideable_type = factor(rideable_type)
  )
```

The four datasets were combined after adding year and month variables.
Year, month, weekday, membership status, and bike type were converted
to factors, with months and weekdays placed in chronological order.

The combined dataset contains `r nrow(citi_df)` observations and
`r ncol(citi_df)` variables. Each row represents one ride, with information
on ride ID, bike type, weekday, duration in minutes, starting and ending
stations, membership status, year, and month. The supplied data contain
1% of rides lasting less than four hours in each of the four months.

There are `r sum(is.na(citi_df$start_station_name))` missing starting
station names and `r sum(is.na(citi_df$end_station_name))` missing ending
station names. These rides are retained for analyses that do not require
station names.

### Ride counts by year, month, and membership

```{r}
citi_df |>
  count(year, month, member_casual) |>
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = member_casual,
    values_from = n,
    values_fill = 0
  ) |>
  knitr::kable(
    col.names = c("Year", "Month", "Casual", "Member")
  )
```

Members account for most rides in all four periods. There are more
sampled rides in July than in January in both years, and more in 2024
than in the corresponding months of 2020. July 2024 has the largest
number of rides, including 36,262 member rides and 10,894 casual rides.
Casual riders also account for a larger proportion of rides in July
than in January.

### Five most popular starting stations in July 2024

```{r}
citi_df |>
  filter(
    year == "2024",
    month == "July",
    !is.na(start_station_name)
  ) |>
  count(start_station_name, sort = TRUE) |>
  slice_head(n = 5) |>
  knitr::kable(
    col.names = c("Starting station", "Number of rides")
  )
```

Pier 61 at Chelsea Piers is the most popular starting station in the
July 2024 sample, with 163 rides. The other leading stations are
University Pl & E 14 St, W 21 St & 6 Ave, West St & Chambers St,
and W 31 St & 7 Ave.

### Median ride duration by weekday, month, and year

```{r, fig.width=10, fig.height=5}
citi_median =
  citi_df |>
  group_by(year, month, weekdays) |>
  summarise(
    median_duration = median(duration),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

citi_median |>
  ggplot(
    aes(
      x = weekdays,
      y = median_duration,
      color = year,
      group = year
    )
  ) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  facet_wrap(~ month) +
  labs(
    title = "Median Ride Duration by Weekday",
    x = "Day of week",
    y = "Median ride duration (minutes)",
    color = "Year"
  ) +
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1)
  )
```
Median ride durations are higher in July than in January and higher in
2020 than in 2024 on every day of the week. In July, weekend rides have
longer median durations than weekday rides, particularly in 2020, when
the weekend medians are approximately 16.5 minutes. January 2020 also
shows longer weekend rides, whereas January 2024 has little variation
across weekdays and no clear weekend increase.
### Ride duration distributions in 2024

```{r, fig.width=10, fig.height=7}
citi_df |>
  filter(year == "2024") |>
  ggplot(
    aes(
      x = duration,
      color = rideable_type,
      fill = rideable_type
    )
  ) +
  geom_density(alpha = 0.2) +
  facet_grid(month ~ member_casual) +
  scale_x_log10(
    breaks = c(1, 5, 10, 30, 60, 120, 240)
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Ride Duration Distributions in 2024",
    x = "Ride duration (minutes; log scale)",
    y = "Density on log-duration scale",
    color = "Bike type",
    fill = "Bike type"
  )
```
Casual riders generally take longer rides than members, and their
ride duration distributions shift toward longer rides in July compared
with January. Among casual riders, classic-bike rides tend to be longer
than electric-bike rides in both months. Among members, the two bike
types have similar distributions in January, while electric-bike rides
tend to be longer in July. Thus, the relationship between bike type and
ride duration differs by membership status. These patterns describe
associations rather than causal effects.
